approved: The majority voted against an [amendment](https://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/download/legislation/amend/r7373_amend_603f7fc6-7a71-4f28-97b0-41468cb73e83/upload_pdf/25075%202R%20T%20OBrien.pdf;fileType=application%2Fpdf) to the usual second reading motion, which is "*that the bill be read a second time*" (parliamentary jargon for agreeing with the main idea of the bill), which means it failed. ### Amendment text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > >> *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House notes that:* >> >> *(1) the Opposition strongly supports the principle of Payday Super;* >> >> *(2) superannuation is part of an employee's wage and must be paid on time;* >> >> *(3) around $5 billion of superannuation goes unpaid every year;* >> >> *(4) the Government has ignored Treasury advice which suggests Digital Service Providers require 18 months from legislating the changes before implementation;* >> >> *(5) the Government is putting small business at risk by rushing the bill's implementation;* >> >> *(6) the Opposition is calling on the Government to delay the start date for small businesses with fewer than 20 employees for 18 months to provide them adequate time to adapt; and* >> >> *(7) the Opposition is calling on the Government to legislate protections for small businesses who have made good faith efforts to comply".*

Moved that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Payday Superannuation) Bill 2025 be read a second time, arguing that superannuation should be paid with wages, strengthening enforcement and redesigning the superannuation guarantee charge to address late or missing contributions.

Moved that the Superannuation Guarantee Charge Amendment Bill 2025 be read a second time, explaining that it would impose the charge for each day wages are paid when contributions are short, alongside payday super reforms.

Argued that superannuation should remain Australians' money and support home ownership, criticised the Treasury Laws Amendment (Payday Superannuation) Bill 2025 for risking small-business insolvencies, and called for the Fair Entitlements Guarantee to cover unpaid superannuation contributions.

Argued that the Treasury Laws Amendment (Payday Superannuation) Bill 2025 will require employers, from 1 July 2026, to pay superannuation guarantee contributions on the same day as wages, helping workers track payments, supporting cash flow and addressing businesses that withhold super. The bill also changes the super guarantee charge and includes transition measures for employers and digital service providers.

Introduced the Treasury Laws Amendment (Payday Superannuation) Bill 2025 and the Superannuation Guarantee Charge Amendment Bill 2025, proposing that superannuation be paid with wages and that enforcement and charge arrangements be redesigned, while opposition speakers supported the principle but criticised the implementation timetable.

Moved amendments concerning superannuation coverage for part-time employees under 18 and asked why employee-onboarding advertising provisions were omitted; the minister said separate stapling and advertising legislation would be introduced in time for the payday super reforms to commence on 1 July.

Moved an amendment to the Treasury Laws Amendment (Payday Superannuation) Bill 2025 to prevent regulations excluding workers under 18 who work fewer than 30 hours from receiving superannuation. Asked about the timing and effect of the bill; the minister said current arrangements would continue until 1 July and rejected changing the system through the amendment.
How did each party vote on the Treasury Laws Amendment (Payday Superannuation) Bill 2025?
